steps: Reduce the whole array with no axis and read the single number.
Reduce with axis=1 and print one value per row.
Compare the shapes: () versus (rows,).
Mean along an axis.realWorld: A dashboard needs both the overall average and the per-customer average; the axis argument is the only difference between them.
mistakes: Assuming axis=1 means "average along the columns".
Expecting a one-element array from the no-axis form.
revision: No axis reduces every element to one scalar.
The named axis is the one that disappears.

steps: Compute std and var on a short array.
Check that std is the square root of var.
Set ddof=1 for the sample form and compare.
Standard deviation and variance.realWorld: Reporting spread in the same units as the data is why std is quoted; var is the intermediate the maths uses.
mistakes: Mixing ddof=0 and ddof=1 across two reports and getting different spreads.
Reading var as if it were in the original units.
revision: var is the mean squared deviation, std its square root.
The default ddof=0 is the population form.

steps: Find where the smallest value sits with argmin.
Produce every running total with cumsum.
Note argmin returns an index and cumsum returns an array.
Position and running totals.realWorld: Finding the worst-performing store and charting cumulative sales in the same report are these two calls.
mistakes: Reading argmin as the minimum value.
Using cumsum where only the final total was needed.
revision: arg* returns a position, the plain reduction returns the value.
cumsum keeps the input length; sum collapses it.

steps: Compute both on a column with one extreme value.
Compare how far each moved from the typical value.
Report both when the distribution may be skewed.
median is not the mean.realWorld: House prices and response times are quoted as medians because one outlier can move the mean by an order of magnitude.
mistakes: Reporting the mean of a skewed column as "typical".
Assuming median sorts the source array — it copies.
revision: median resists extremes; mean does not.
Comparing the two is how a skew is noticed.

steps: Reduce rows with and without keepdims.
Print both shapes: (2,) versus (2, 1).
Divide the matrix by the kept column and confirm the shapes match.
keepdims keeps a column.realWorld: Normalising every row by its own total needs the divisor as a column, and keepdims produces exactly that with no reshape.
mistakes: Using the flat (2,) result as a divisor and getting a ValueError.
Adding a reshape that duplicates what keepdims already did.
revision: keepdims leaves the reduced axis as length 1.
The result broadcasts straight back against the input.

steps: Compute a plain mean of two values.
Compute a weighted mean with one weight three times the other.
Check the result moved toward the heavier value.
average can weight values.realWorld: Survey results weighted by population, and grades weighted by credit, are one call rather than a manual sum of products.
mistakes: Passing weights whose length differs from the data.
Forgetting the denominator is the weight total, not the count.
revision: average is sum(w*x) / sum(w).
Equal weights reduce to the plain mean.

steps: Build a boolean array with one True.
Ask any and all and print both answers.
State the rule: any needs one True, all needs every True.
any and all answer yes/no.realWorld: A validation gate asks "did any row fail?" with any and "did every row pass?" with all — one call each, no loop.
mistakes: Calling any on a numeric array and counting non-zeros by accident.
Confusing all with a check that the array is non-empty.
revision: any and all reduce a boolean array to one Python bool.
On a numeric array, zero counts as False.

steps: Multiply a short integer array with prod.
Check the result against the hand product.
Watch the dtype when the numbers are large.
prod multiplies the elements.realWorld: Compound growth factors multiply across periods, so the cumulative return is a prod of (1 + r) terms.
mistakes: Overflowing a small integer dtype on a long array.
Using prod where a sum was meant and getting a meaningless total.
revision: prod folds with multiplication instead of addition.
The dtype of the accumulator matters for long products.

steps: Reduce a 2×2 matrix with no axis.
Print the value and its type.
Confirm it is a scalar, not a (1, 1) array.
mean of a matrix returns one number.realWorld: A single KPI across every cell — overall conversion, global error — is the no-axis reduction, and it flattens first.
mistakes: Indexing the result as if it were an array.
Assuming no-axis reduction averages the row means.
revision: No axis flattens before reducing.
The result is a NumPy scalar, printable and comparable.

steps: Sum a (2, 3) matrix along axis 1.
Print the result and confirm it has length 2.
Check the first value against a hand sum of the first row.
axis=1 reduces each row.realWorld: A per-order total from a line-item matrix is a row reduction; the order count stays, the line-item axis goes.
mistakes: Expecting a column-shaped result from axis=1.
Mixing up which axis disappeared.
revision: The named axis is removed from the result.
axis=1 keeps one value per row.

steps: Compute std on a small array.
Compare it with the variance of the same data.
Note the units: std is in the data's scale, var is squared.
std measures spread in the same units.realWorld: Error bars and quality bands are quoted as ±1 std because that number is in the same unit as the measurement.
mistakes: Quoting the variance with the data's unit label.
Comparing std of two columns measured in different units.
revision: std is the square root of variance.
Only std carries the original unit.

steps: Print the maximum value.
Print the index argmax returns for the same array.
Add an axis and confirm both return one answer per row.
The maximum and where it lives.realWorld: A leaderboard needs the top score and its holder: max gives the score, argmax gives the row to look up the name.
mistakes: Using argmax as the value.
Forgetting argmax returns the FIRST maximum when there are ties.
revision: max is a value, argmax is a position.
Both accept axis for per-row answers.

steps: Sum a (2, 3) matrix along axis 0 and print the shape.
Sum the same matrix along axis 1 and print the shape.
Map each result back to "per column" and "per row".
axis=0 sums columns, axis=1 sums rows.realWorld: Feature totals per column and record totals per row are the same call with a different axis, and most aggregation bugs are this one choice.
mistakes: Reading axis=0 as "sum the rows".
Expecting the surviving axis to keep its original position.
revision: The axis you name is the one that disappears.
axis=0 collapses rows, so one value per column survives.

steps: Ask for the median as the 50th percentile.
Ask for the quartiles as a list and compare the values.
Note the default linear interpolation between order statistics.
Percentiles answer rank questions.realWorld: Latency SLOs are stated as p95 and p99; the mean would hide the slow tail those percentiles expose.
mistakes: Passing 50 instead of 0.5 to quantile — percentile and quantile use different scales.
Assuming the percentile is always one of the observed values.
revision: percentile takes 0–100; quantile takes 0–1.
Interpolation means the answer can sit between two data points.

steps: Build the comparison mask from the array.
Index the array with that mask.
Print the passing values and note the result is shorter.
Filter with a mask.realWorld: Pass lists, alert queues and eligible rows all come from one comparison plus one index — the mask is the query.
mistakes: Using the mask as a scalar boolean.
Assuming the filtered array keeps the original shape.
revision: The comparison builds a mask of the same shape.
Indexing with it returns only the True positions, flattened.

steps: Write the condition as a boolean array.
Pass the two branch values to where.
Print the result and confirm it has the condition's shape.
np.where chooses without a loop.realWorld: Labelling a column pass/fail or capping an outlier is a vectorised if/else, which keeps the transformation in one expression.
mistakes: Passing only the condition and getting indices instead of values.
Expecting the branches to be evaluated lazily.
revision: where(condition, x, y) is an elementwise choice.
Both branches are evaluated, so keep them cheap.

steps: Build the membership mask with isin.
Print it and check it matches the array's shape.
Compose it with another mask using &.
Membership with isin.realWorld: Keeping only known country codes or valid SKUs is an isin filter, which replaces a loop with an `in` test per row.
mistakes: Using `element in list` inside a comprehension.
Assuming isin mutates the array.
revision: isin returns a boolean mask, not the values.
The mask composes with & and | like any other.

steps: Build two comparisons and wrap each in parentheses.
Combine them with & for both-true.
Filter the array with the combined mask.
Combine masks with & and |.realWorld: A price range, a date window or an age band is two comparisons combined elementwise, never a Python `and`.
mistakes: Using `and`, which raises on an array.
Omitting the parentheses, so & binds before the comparison.
revision: Elementwise logic uses & and |, not and and or.
Each comparison needs its own parentheses.

steps: Build a mask and print what it keeps.
Invert it with ~ and index again.
Confirm the two results partition the array.
Invert a mask with ~.realWorld: The held-out split of a dataset is the negation of the training mask, so one mask defines both halves without a second comparison.
mistakes: Using `not` on an array.
Forgetting the parentheses before the tilde.
revision: ~ flips every boolean value.
A mask and its negation partition the array.

steps: Build a mask for the values to replace.
Assign the replacement on the left of the mask.
Print the array and confirm only those cells changed.
Assign through a mask.realWorld: Clamping negatives to zero before a ratio or a log is one masked assignment, and the rest of the column keeps its values.
mistakes: Writing a[a < 0] == 0, which compares instead of assigning.
Assigning an array whose length differs from the selected cells.
revision: A mask on the left assigns in place.
The number of selected cells must match the value count.

steps: Build the mask.
Sum it and print the count.
Wrap in int() when a Python number is needed.
Count how many match.realWorld: Missing-value counts, failed-record counts and pass rates are all a summed mask, which needs no filtering at all.
mistakes: Filtering first and then calling len, which allocates a new array.
Forgetting the count returns a NumPy integer.
revision: True counts as 1, so a sum is a count.
No new array is needed to count matches.

steps: Build a mask from a single column.
Apply it to the whole matrix.
Confirm every column of the selected rows came along.
Filter rows by one column.realWorld: Filtering records by one field while keeping the other fields is the standard table filter, and the mask only needs the row count.
mistakes: Applying a column mask to every cell instead of to the rows.
Using the column's own shape in a place that expects the row count.
revision: A 1-D row mask selects whole rows.
The mask length must equal the number of rows.

steps: Compare an array with a number and print the mask's shape.
Check it equals the source's shape.
Note that only indexing with the mask shortens the data.
A mask keeps the shape of its array.realWorld: Storing a mask beside its source only makes sense while the shapes agree, which is why a mask is invalidated by any filter.
mistakes: Reusing a mask after the array was filtered.
Expecting the comparison itself to drop non-matching values.
revision: A comparison returns a same-shape boolean array.
Filtering is the indexing step, not the comparison.

steps: Choose between two literal values with one condition.
Print the result and its dtype.
Swap the branches and compare the output.
where chooses between two values.realWorld: A vectorised label column — big/small, up/down, ok/late — is a single where instead of a list comprehension with an if.
mistakes: Mixing branch dtypes and getting an unexpected upcast.
Assuming where short-circuits and skips a branch.
revision: where is an elementwise if/else.
Output dtype follows the promotion of both branches.

steps: Build the comparison.
Sum it to get the count.
Compare with the length of the filtered array.
Sum the mask to count matches.realWorld: A quick "how many rows qualify" before running an expensive query is a summed mask — no array is materialised.
mistakes: Using len on the mask, which returns the array length.
Leaving the result as a NumPy scalar in a JSON payload.
revision: sum on a mask counts the True values.
int() converts it for Python-side use.

steps: Build a full-shape mask for the matrix.
Index the matrix with it.
Print the result and note it is 1-D.
Filter a matrix elementwise.realWorld: Collecting every qualifying cell across a table — all outliers anywhere — uses an elementwise mask, while keeping rows needs a row mask.
mistakes: Expecting the rectangle to survive elementwise filtering.
Using an elementwise mask where whole rows were intended.
revision: A full-shape mask flattens the matches into 1-D.
Row masks are the way to keep the other columns attached.

steps: Build a condition and two same-shape value arrays.
Apply where and print the mixed result.
Confirm each cell came from the branch the condition selected.
where chooses between two arrays.realWorld: Choosing between a capped and an uncapped value per cell, from two computed columns, is one where instead of a loop with indexing.
mistakes: Passing branches of different shapes that cannot broadcast.
Assuming where evaluates the branches lazily.
revision: Both branches are arrays and both broadcast with the condition.
The output shape is the broadcast shape.

steps: Build the mask for the values to change.
Assign on the left of the mask.
Print the array to confirm the untouched values survived.
Updating through a mask.realWorld: Sentinel values, negative readings and impossible ages are cleaned in place with one masked assignment.
mistakes: Comparing with == instead of assigning with =.
Assigning a scalar of a dtype that cannot hold the remaining values.
revision: The mask selects the cells that the assignment rewrites.
Everything outside the mask keeps its value.
